newsitem.title: USA: Brady bonds slump as rally runs out of steam.
newsitem.headline: Brady bonds slump as rally runs out of steam.

text.p: Emerging debt prices slumped Monday as dealers and investors flocked out of a market that had posted a strong rally over recent weeks, traders said.

Brady bond traders linked the weakness to uncertainty over an Argentine debt buyback and concerns about the spillover effect of Asian foreign exchange turmoil, but added that any unwinding would be seen as natural.

"When it started heading lower, the market just caved in. There was no real support here," one Brady bond trader said. "It's not the end of the world, a lot of people have been calling for it for a week or so."
In earlier weeks, the Brady bond market had tightened to historically tight spreads against U.S. Treasuries and many analysts saw the recent widening as inevitable.
"The market has had such a good run that people are starting to take profits," Walter Molano, director of Latin American economic research at SBC Warburg.
Comments from Argentine Finance Ministry Undersecretary Miguel Kiguel that a debt buyback was not imminent undermined Argentine paper, traders said.

Argentina announced that it would issue a $750 million seven year global bond due via CS First Boston and SBC Warburg, but traders said the deal may have deflated hopes Buenos Aires swap existing Bradies for new long term paper.
Brazilian debt suffered, as the Bovespa dropped sharply, and the local market felt ongoing nervousness that the recent Asian currency instability might pressure the Brazilian real.

Over the past two weeks, the Thai and Philippine authorities implemented effective devaluations of the baht and the peso, and these situations issued had sharpened questions about Brazil's growing current account deficit.

Brazil reported its current account in the past 12 months to June widened to 4.19 percent of GDP, up from 4.07 in the 12 months to May. The central bank said it expected the gap to grow to about 4.5 percent of GDP by year end.
"It showed a continuation of gradual deterioration int he number," said Tulio Vera, managing director at Bear Stearns, who added that the comparisons between brazil and Thailand had been exaggerated.
"What you're seeing is an excuse to take profits," Vera said. "I don't see a lot of parallels between some of the Asian situations and the Brazilian situation."
